{{Short description|Young child with an aptitude for the game of chess}}
[[File:Fairbanks Chaplin Reshevsky 1921.jpg|300px|thumb|right|[[Samuel Reshevsky]] playing chess with [[Douglas Fairbanks]], as [[Charlie Chaplin]] watches them during filming of the American silent film ''[[The Three Musketeers (1921 film)|The Three Musketeers]]'', 1921]]
A '''chess prodigy''' is a young child who possesses an aptitude for [[chess]] that far exceeds what might be expected at their age. Their [[Child prodigy|prodigious]] talent will often enable them to defeat experienced adult players and even titled chess masters. Some chess prodigies have progressed to become grandmasters or even [[World Chess Championship|World Chess Champions]].

In 1950, [[FIDE]] introduced the titles of [[international master]] (IM) and [[Grandmaster (chess)|grandmaster]] (GM). One measure of chess prodigies is the age at which they earn each of these titles. In the below tables, the ages listed are the ages at which a player qualified for a title. This is not equal to the age at which they officially earned the title, because GM and IM titles can only be awarded at [[FIDE]] congresses. The country listed indicates the federation the player was affiliated with at the time of gaining the title, not their current or later affiliation.

== Early chess prodigies ==

Early chess prodigies included [[Paul Morphy]] (1837–1884) and [[José Raúl Capablanca]] (1888–1942), both of whom won matches against strong adult opponents at the age of 12, and [[Samuel Reshevsky]] (1911–1992), who gave [[simultaneous exhibition]]s at the age of six.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chessbase.com/newsdetail.asp?newsid=2858|title=Chess prodigies and mini-grandmasters|date=10 January 2006|access-date=8 August 2017}}</ref> Morphy went on to become the world's leading player before the formal [[World chess championship|World Champion]] title existed. Capablanca became the third World Champion, and Reshevsky, while never becoming World Champion, was among the world's elite players for many decades.

[[Arturo Pomar]] (1931–2016) was another to be labelled a prodigy by chess writers.<ref>{{cite book | author=Saidy, Anthony | author-link=Anthony Saidy | author2=Lessing, Norman | author2-link=Norman Lessing | title=The World of Chess | publisher=William Collins Sons & Co. Ltd. | year=1974 | isbn=0-394-48777-X | page=13}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=Whyld, Kenneth | title=Guinness Chess, The Records | publisher=Guinness Publishing Ltd | year=1986 | isbn= 0851124550 | page=259}}</ref> He played his first international tournament (Madrid 1943) at the age of 11 and went on to become Spain's first [[Grandmaster (chess)|grandmaster]].

[[Jutta Hempel]] (born 1960) at the age of 6 played 12 simultaneous games and won 9.5-2.5.<ref name="CB">[https://en.chessbase.com/post/the-beth-harmon-that-almost-was ChessBase: The Beth Harmon that Almost was], [[Chessbase]], July 24, 2022</ref>

===Speed Chess===

Including FIDE-rated [[Rapid chess|rapid]] and [[Blitz chess|blitz]] games, [[Roman Shogdzhiev]] from Russia defeated grandmasters [[Jakhongir Vakhidov]] and [[Johan-Sebastian Christiansen]] in the [[World Rapid Chess Championship 2023|World Rapid Championship 2023]], and after a couple of days defeated GMs [[Kirill Shevchenko]], [[Alan Pichot]] and [[Pranav V]] in the [[World Blitz Chess Championship 2023|World Blitz Championship 2023]]. He was 8 years, 10 months, and 22-26 days at the time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Svensen (TarjeiJS) |first=Tarjei J. |date=2024-01-08 |title=8-Year-Old Roman Shogdzhiev Amazes Chess World By Beating 5 Grandmasters |url=https://www.chess.com/news/view/roman-shogdzhiev-beats-five-grandmasters |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Chess.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Youngest international master ==
In general, the IM title is awarded to players who achieve a [[FIDE Rating|FIDE rating]] of at least 2400 and three IM norms, which are tournament results with a [[Performance rating (chess)|performance rating]] of at least 2450 over 9 or more games. == Youngest grandmaster ==

=== List of record-holders ===
Below are players who have held the record for the youngest grandmaster. The first record holder was [[David Bronstein]], who was the youngest of the 27 inaugural players to be awarded the title by [[FIDE]] in 1950 at age 26. The requirements for earning the GM title have changed over time.<ref name="WallFIDEHistory">{{cite web |url=http://www.geocities.com/SiliconValley/Lab/7378/fide.htm|title=FIDE History|last=Wall|first=W|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091028083110/http://www.geocities.com/SiliconValley/Lab/7378/fide.htm|archive-date=2009-10-28}}</ref> In the present system, the title is awarded to players who achieve a [[FIDE Rating|FIDE rating]] of at least 2500 and three GM norms.<ref name=":2" /> The current record-holder is [[Abhimanyu Mishra]] of the United States, who qualified for the title at age 12 years, 4 months, and 25 days in 2021.

The current record-holder is [[Yağız Kaan Erdoğmuş]] of Turkey at the age of 14 years, 10 months, and 28 days. In April 2026, he defeated former World Champion [[Veselin Topalov]] 5–1 in the "Clash of Generations III" match  to reach a live rating of 2709.4.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Svensen (TarjeiJS) |first=Tarjei J. |date=2026-04-18 |title=Erdogmus Scores 5-1 Knockout Against Topalov, Closes In On Youngest-Ever 2700 Record |url=https://www.chess.com/news/view/erdogmus-makes-history-again-to-become-youngest-ever-2700-player |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Chess.com |language=en-US}}</ref>
